query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous high-temperature wear and corrosive conditions, the mechanically induced dynamic amorphization of the multi‐phase eutectic HEA generates an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer with a high density of high-energy grain boundaries, which in turn accelerates corrosion. This process creates a positive feedback loop where wear promotes microstructural changes that enhance corrosion, and the resulting corrosion damage further compromises the mechanical integrity, accelerating wear.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a designed, heterogeneous microstructure that has not yet undergone dynamic amorphization or surface refinement.
generation.intervention: Exposure of the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosion under elevated temperature conditions (e.g., in an oxidizing environment).
generation.conditions: High temperature sufficient to accelerate oxidation kinetics; presence of a corrosive medium that facilitates electrochemical attack; and mechanical wear applied concurrently.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized near-surface layer characterized by increased grain boundary density and higher grain boundary energies.
generation.mechanism: Wear-induced dynamic amorphization creates a finer-grained surface with an abundance of reactive grain boundaries. At elevated temperatures, these grain boundaries serve as preferential sites for corrosion (oxide formation or localized attack). This leads to accelerated degradation because the corrosion further softens the surface, making it more vulnerable to wear, thus establishing a coupled degradation cycle.
generation.predicted_outcome: Total degradation will be higher relative to a baseline condition where only wear or corrosion acts alone, with a significant increase in corrosion rate due to the additional reactive sites, and a moderate increase in wear due to the compromised structural integrity. The synergistic effect results in faster overall material loss.
generation.baseline: A matched multi-phase eutectic HEA undergoing either isolated wear or isolated corrosion at similar elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for conditions where temperatures are sufficiently high to promote oxidation and dynamic microstructural transformation. In inert or low-temperature environments where oxidation is limited, the coupled acceleration effect may not be evident.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of wear versus corrosion to the overall degradation rate and the exact kinetics of the dynamic amorphization process remain uncertain. Moreover, the specific microstructural evolution under simultaneous loading requires further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples. Group A will receive the standard processing and be exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature. Group B will be pre-treated (e.g., via surface annealing or stabilization treatments) to inhibit dynamic amorphization. Both groups will be subjected to identical testing conditions. Post-test analyses will include quantification of total material loss, separate assessments of wear track volume and corrosion extent, and detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or STEM metrics of grain boundary density).
measurements: Total material loss (weight loss, volume loss)
Wear track geometry and volume (via profilometry or 3D microscopy)
Corrosion kinetics (electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, polarization curves)
Microstructural analysis of the surface layer (TEM/STEM imaging, grain boundary density measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Group B (with microstructure stabilization) does not exhibit a significantly reduced coupled degradation rate compared to Group A, or if no statistically significant increase in near-surface grain boundary density is observed in Group A, then the hypothesis that wear-induced dynamic amorphization accelerates corrosion (and thus overall degradation) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
